proposition: Ninety-nine is not a fact about forts. It is a general-purpose Rigvedic quantity that forts are one of several kinds of thing to take.
evidence_for: The náva- 1 + navatí- expression co-occurs in 19 stanzas; on a strict reading, where the expression yields 99 as the quantity of the object, 16. Forts take it in 6 - well under half either way. The rest are rivers (1.32.14, 10.104.8), Vr̥tras (1.84.13), arms (2.14.4), horses (4.48.4), a serpent's coils (5.29.6), ramparts (6.47.2), unnamed broken things (9.61.1), gifts (10.39.10) and the mighty (10.49.8). Nothing links that list except the number. RV 10.104.8 carries the expression counting streams AND the epithet pūrbhít 'fort-breaker' in one stanza. The twelve non-fort uses span seven books (1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10) and at least five Arnold strata, so they are not a local mannerism of one book or poet. Ninety-nine is also not modal: nine passages state a śatá- count against six for 99 (DJ-015).
evidence_against: The number does not float free of narrative: 99 and 100 sort to Divodāsa, Atithigva and Śambara, while 7 goes with Purukutsa and the Pūru in all four of their passages (PUR4J finding 5). Ornament does not sort by story, so a quantity used for nine kinds of object is still doing something when it is chosen. And the denominator is small: 16 to 19 stanzas supports a claim about usage, not a law.
what_it_does_not_establish: It does not establish that no Rigvedic fort count records anything historical - a formulaic number can be attached to a remembered event, and one of the six could be. It does not establish WHY ninety-nine: a decimal-adjacent maximum, a one-short-of-a-hundred completion (two of the six add 'the hundredth'), and a stock epic quantity are all live and none is tested here.
falsifier: Falsified by a count outside the stock - a 23 or a 41 - attached to a fort, which would show the corpus can state an arbitrary number and chooses not to. Weakened if the six fort uses prove separable from the rest by stratum or dialect. The book-and-stratum spread reported above is a crude test and a finer one could still find structure.
notes: This SUPERSEDES nothing in PUR4J-I-01, which reached a compatible conclusion from one control case. It widens the base and is recorded separately because the widening is this unit's. AMENDED after adversarial review: the earlier row said 'forts are 6 of 19 - under a third' without noting that three of the nineteen (1.53.9, 1.191.13, 10.98.10) do not yield 99 as the quantity of the object. The strict denominator is 16.

proposition: The corpus supplies no lexical evidence in its gloss column that a púr- was a brick-built city - and a translator inside the same corpus supplies both words at the two most consequential passages. The absences are not decisive and neither is the presence.
evidence_for: No lemma is glossed 'brick' or 'city' against a 91.7% lemma / 78.98% token denominator (DJ-008). The gloss column's own entry for púr- is an earthwork - 'Wall aus Steinen und Lehm, Verschanzung, Palisade' - not a city. 67.5% of simplex tokens are accusative and 3.6% locative: the commonest thing a púr does is be the object of a verb of breaking (DJ-006). The corpus has abundant settlement vocabulary that is NOT púr- (DJ-012). No lemma is glossed for the act of building (DJ-009).
evidence_against: FOUR ITEMS, THREE OF THEM ADDED OR STRENGTHENED BY ADVERSARIAL REVIEW. (1) Renou, in the same pinned corpus, renders RV 2.35.6 'Dans les forteresses (en briques) crues' - unfired BRICK, at the one púr- passage that states a material - and RV 1.173.10 'maître de la cité', lord of the CITY (DJ-013). Both words DJ-008 records as absent from the gloss column are supplied by a translation inside the corpus, at the two locators where it matters most. (2) The corpus carries the fired/unfired opposition that brick technology turns on - pakvá- 'gebacken' 25 tokens against āmá- 'roh, ungekocht' 11 - and puts the unfired term on a fort (DJ-009). (3) RV 6.2.7 'like an old man in a fort' and RV 9.107.10 'as a body of troops enters the fort' are similes, and a simile draws on what its audience finds ordinary, so both PRESUPPOSE the inhabited fort the corpus never asserts (DJ-007). (4) pū́rpati- 'lord of the fort' is one token and is itself inside a simile (DJ-014), which cuts both ways and is recorded on both sides.
what_it_does_not_establish: It does not establish that Rigvedic púr- were small, temporary or non-urban. It does not establish that brick was unknown to the composers - and after DJ-009 and DJ-013 it cannot be read that way at all. It does not settle whether púr- and the Harappan citadel are the same object: that is HYP-J-001, and the answer there is that this repository cannot tell.
falsifier: Falsified in the deflationary direction by a lemma glossed 'brick' or 'city' in a lexicon independent of the Zurich column, which would also show the single-source dependency was doing the work. Moved substantially by Sāyaṇa or any pre-modern commentary on the ten material passages, and by a survey of what pakvá- and āmá- modify elsewhere in the corpus, which was not run.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/domain-j-measurements.csv DJ-006 to DJ-009 and DJ-012 to DJ-014; 03-REGISTERS/HYPOTHESIS-ELIGIBILITY.csv HYP-J-001
notes: THE PROPOSITION OF THIS ROW WAS REWRITTEN TWICE, BOTH TIMES AWAY FROM THE SAME CONVENIENT CONCLUSION. The first draft asserted 'no word for brick, no word for city, therefore not a Harappan city' and was corrected by the two similes (BF-016). The second still read 'no positive lexical evidence ... and no evidence that it was not', which adversarial review showed was false in its own corpus: Renou's 'briques crues' and the pakvá-/āmá- pair are positive evidence, and the unit had retrieved both and read neither (BF-017). The pattern is the finding: the deflationary reading survived two drafts because the checks that would break it were not run, and both times they were free.

proposition: The English word 'fort' is not a translation of a Rigvedic category. It is a bracket that several Sanskrit words fall into and out of, and where the bracket is contested the translators are contested too.
evidence_for: The great majority of the 21 durgá- tokens denote difficult ground or peril rather than a fortification, and the recurrent construction is a prayer to be carried across one (DJ-011). dehī́- 'Aufwurf, Damm, Wall' - an earth-heap from √dih 'smear, plaster up' - takes the same ninety-nine expression and the same opponent as púr- but sits outside the register by an etymological rule (DJ-005). The gloss column's púr- is an earthwork or palisade, not a city. Translators diverge on the same word within one corpus: at RV 2.35.6 Griffith has 'forts unwrought', Geldner 'rohen Burgen' and Renou 'forteresses (en briques) crues'; at RV 1.173.10 Griffith 'some city's lord', Geldner 'Burgherren', Renou 'maître de la cité' (DJ-013).
evidence_against: THE ABSOLUTE FORM OF THE durgá- CLAIM IS FALSE AND THE FALSIFIER THIS ROW DECLARED HAS FIRED. At RV 5.34.7 all three of Griffith, Geldner and Grassmann render durgá- as a fortified place people hold out in, and at RV 5.54.4 they disagree with each other. Two further passages are unresolved (RV 4.28.3, 7.25.2). The durgá- base is also thinner than 21 suggests: six tokens are one refrain and RV 7.60.12 and 7.61.7 are word for word identical, so there are at most 15 distinct formulations. Separately, the earlier version of this row said grā́ma- is 'a moving war-band in Grassmann's Rigvedic gloss' - false twice over: the gloss is the Zurich column's, not Grassmann's, and it reads '... wehrhafte Mannschaft einer Siedlung, Dorfgemeinde, bewohnter Platz', carrying the village sense the row denied by truncating the quotation (DJ-012).
what_it_does_not_establish: It does not establish what any of these words did mean, only that the English bracket does not carry evenly across them. It does not license replacing 'fort' with 'earthwork' as a new default gloss - that would repeat the error in the other direction. It does not establish that durgá- is never a fortification in the Rigveda; RV 5.34.7 is evidence that it sometimes is.
falsifier: For durgá-, the strong form is ALREADY FALSIFIED at RV 5.34.7. The surviving weak form - that difficult ground is the dominant sense - would be falsified by a majority of the remaining passages reading as fortifications under a lexicon independent of the Zurich column, or by a pre-modern commentary reading them so.
notes: §7 names 'fort' among the inherited English categories to audit before use. This row is the audit at the level of the category. It is PROVISIONAL and its strongest single item has been withdrawn: the claim that no durgá- is ever held was the load-bearing anti-Nandi result, it was shipped VERIFIED, and it was contradicted by a translation file the unit had already retrieved and cited.
